briefing.headline: UK and US political tensions rise over policy and courts
briefing.overview: Britain’s government faces pressure on tuition fees, devolution and Heathrow expansion, while US courts clash with political parties over campaign advertising and free‑speech rules.

stories.title: Burnham rejects equal tuition fees for EU students
stories.what_happened: Prime Minister Mark Burnham said the UK will not offer the same tuition fees to EU students and described negotiations with the EU as ongoing. The statement was made at a press conference on 25 Nov 2026.
stories.why_it_matters: The issue tests the limits of executive power in setting education policy after Brexit, linking to the A‑level topic of the Constitution and the role of the Prime Minister. It also raises questions about the UK’s international obligations.

perspectives.label: Supporters argue
perspectives.text: Pro‑government voices say the policy protects UK taxpayers and reflects sovereign control over immigration.

perspectives.label: Critics argue
perspectives.text: Opposition parties claim it breaches the spirit of the EU‑UK partnership and harms student mobility.

perspectives.label: From the left
perspectives.text: Left‑leaning groups warn it creates a two‑tier system that disadvantages poorer EU students.

key_term.definition: The ability of the Prime Minister and Cabinet to make policy decisions without needing prior parliamentary approval.

stories.exam_use: Use as evidence in a constitutional essay on the balance of power between the executive and external agreements.

stories.title: Plaid Cymru calls for a New Deal for Wales
stories.what_happened: Plaid Cymru launched a petition on 26 Nov 2026 demanding the UK government grant Wales powers comparable to Scotland’s. The petition cites policing, justice and rail as key areas.
stories.why_it_matters: The demand illustrates the ongoing debate over the distribution of powers within the UK, a core part of the AQA topic on Devolution and the principle of subsidiarity.

perspectives.label: From the right
perspectives.text: Conservatives argue further devolution would fragment the UK and weaken national cohesion.

perspectives.label: From the left
perspectives.text: Welsh nationalists contend it would enable more democratic accountability and regional development.

perspectives.label: Supporters argue
perspectives.text: Pro‑devolution advocates say it respects the distinct identity and needs of Wales.

key_term.definition: The principle that decisions should be taken at the most local level possible.

stories.exam_use: Cite in a comparative essay on devolution versus centralisation in the UK.

stories.title: Judge rejects DNC claim over taxpayer‑funded Trump ads
stories.what_happened: On 26 Nov 2026 a federal judge ruled against the Democratic National Committee in a case about the use of taxpayer money for pro‑Trump advertisements. The decision favoured the administration’s position.
stories.why_it_matters: The ruling highlights the judiciary’s role in interpreting campaign‑finance law, relevant to the A‑level topic on US Courts and separation of powers.

perspectives.label: Democrats argue
perspectives.text: The DNC says the decision undermines fair competition and free speech.

perspectives.label: Republicans argue
perspectives.text: Republicans claim the ruling protects lawful government communication.

perspectives.label: From the left
perspectives.text: Progressive commentators warn it sets a precedent for partisan use of public funds.

key_term.definition: A process by which courts examine the legality of actions taken by the executive or legislature.

stories.exam_use: Use as evidence in an essay on the checks and balances between US courts and the executive.

stories.title: Federal judge blocks FCC action against ABC
stories.what_happened: A US district judge on 26 Nov 2026 ruled that the FCC violated ABC’s free‑speech rights by attempting to punish the network for satire of former President Trump. The injunction halted the FCC’s enforcement.
stories.why_it_matters: The case illustrates the tension between regulatory authority and First‑Amendment protections, a key issue in the AQA civil‑rights syllabus.

perspectives.label: Free‑speech advocates argue
perspectives.text: The decision safeguards media independence and the right to political satire.

perspectives.label: Regulators argue
perspectives.text: The FCC maintains it was enforcing standards against misinformation.

perspectives.label: From the left
perspectives.text: Progressive groups view the ruling as a victory for democratic discourse.

key_term.definition: The US constitutional guarantee of freedom of speech, press, religion, assembly and petition.

stories.exam_use: Reference in a civil‑rights essay on the balance between regulation and free expression.

stories.title: Committee says Heathrow runway case weak on climate
stories.what_happened: On 26 Nov 2026 the Transport Committee reported that ministers had failed to justify a third runway at Heathrow, citing shortcomings against economic and climate pledges. MPs were urged to reconsider the proposal.
stories.why_it_matters: The report demonstrates parliamentary scrutiny of executive proposals, linking to the AQA focus on Parliament’s role in policy making and accountability.

perspectives.label: Environmentalists argue
perspectives.text: The runway would breach the UK’s net‑zero commitments.

perspectives.label: Business supporters argue
perspectives.text: Proponents claim it would boost the economy and jobs.

perspectives.label: From the right
perspectives.text: Conservatives stress the need for infrastructure to maintain global competitiveness.

key_term.definition: The process by which Parliament examines and challenges the actions of the government.

stories.exam_use: Use as evidence in an essay on how parliamentary committees hold the executive to account.

compare.uk: The UK Prime Minister uses executive discretion to set tuition‑fee policy, a decision that can be challenged by Parliament and devolved administrations.
compare.us: The US President’s campaign advertising is subject to judicial review, with courts able to limit executive use of public funds for political messaging.
compare.insight: Both systems show that executives are not absolute; they are checked by other branches—Parliament in the UK and the judiciary in the US.

ideas_lens.text: Burnham’s tuition‑fee stance reflects liberalism’s emphasis on individual responsibility and limited state intervention, echoing John Stuart Mill’s arguments for minimal government interference in personal affairs.

exam_question.question: Assess the extent to which executive power is checked by other institutions in the UK and the US, using recent examples.
exam_question.tip: Structure your answer by comparing parliamentary oversight in the UK with judicial review in the US, citing the Heathrow committee report and the US court ruling on campaign ads.
